initial_observation.encounter_context: attended a routine optician appointment, which raised concerns about papilloedema
initial_observation.chief_complaint: no symptoms; asymptomatic presentation with incidental concern about papilloedema
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: A routine optician appointment raised concerns about papilloedema (subsequently diagnosed as drusen). A non-enhanced head CT demonstrated a well-demarcated hyperdense lesion in the left posterior frontal lobe with surrounding hypodensity suggesting oedema. MRI brain showed a lesion with features in keeping with Baló’s concentric sclerosis with alternating circular layers of high and low density giving the appearance of an onion bulb. The child was managed conservatively.

evidence_items.source_text: A non-enhanced head CT demonstrated a well-demarcated hyperdense lesion in the left posterior frontal lobe with surrounding hypodensity suggesting oedema. On MRI brain, the lesion had features in keeping with Baló’s concentric sclerosis with alternating circular layers of high and low density giving the appearance of an onion bulb (figure 1A–C).

Serial MRI brain scans at presentation (A–C), 3 months (D–F) and 6 months (G–I) following initial presentation in a child with Baló’s concentric sclerosis. The initial MRI with contrast demonstrated a T2 hyperintense abnormality with central hypointense ring-like focus (A); alternating layers of high and low signal intensity giving it an ‘onion bulb’ appearance. There was central concentric contrast enhancement (B). At 3 months, the extent of the abnormality (D) and the area of contrast enhancement (E) had increased. At 6 months, the abnormality (G) and the contrast enhancement (H) had resolved. The abnormality showed central diffusion restriction with unrestricted diffusion in the periphery (C). The area of diffusion restriction increased in size at 3 months (F) and disappeared by 6 months (I).
evidence_items.temporal_cue: presentation and 3 months and 6 months later

evidence_items.source_text: Advanced neuroimaging (figure 2A–C) supported the probable benign nature of the lesion, but repeat imaging, 3 months later, demonstrated an increase in the size and change in signal characteristics of the lesion (figure 1D–F) leading to the decision to biopsy and exclude a tumour.
Histopathological examination confirmed a demyelinating inflammatory lesion (figure 3A–D).

H&E staining, supplemented by Luxol fast blue staining, confirmed the presence of an inflammatory demyelinating lesion with an obvious transition between preserved white matter and demyelinated white matter. Affected white matter showed reactive gliosis and prominent lymphocytic activity. This was evident in the form of striking perivascular cuffs of lymphocytes with an additional component of dispersed parenchymal inflammation accompanying phagocytosing macrophage activity, the latter though not seen as confluent sheets of macrophages. Limited numbers of perivascular plasma cells were also present. The lymphocytes were predominantly T lymphocytes (mainly CD8 positive, but with a CD4 contribution), but some cuffs of perivascular inflammation were contributed by an outer cuff of B lymphocytes. Both B and T cell populations lacked cytological atypia. No evidence of vasculitis was found. Neurofilament protein immunostaining (not illustrated) showed that axons were generally preserved with little axonal loss. Beta-APP immunostaining highlighted some axonal injury seen as axonal bulbs and threads. In the demyelinated areas, there was a decreased density of axons due to a combination of some axonal loss and separation by oedema. Nuclear Ki-67 labelling (not illustrated) colocalised to inflammatory foci and did not raise a significant concern of underlying lymphoma given the absence of atypical immunopositive nuclear profiles.

Routine blood tests were unremarkable. Examination of the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) was normal including PCR (polymerase chain reaction) for viral pathogens; oligoclonal bands were not present. A serum autoantibody screen including antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, anticardiolipin, and aquaporin-4 antibodies were all negative; serum complement levels were normal. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was mildly elevated (13 mm in 1 hour), but the child had tonsillitis at the time.
evidence_items.temporal_cue: on initial evaluation after lesion detection

evidence_items.source_text: Dynamic susceptibility contrast (DSC) perfusion imaging, magnetic resonance spectroscopy and white matter tractography images. (A) DSC perfusion imaging in a child with Baló’s concentric sclerosis demonstrates that the relative cerebral blood flow within the demyelinating lesion is equal to that of the contralateral normal brain parenchyma. (B) Magnetic resonance spectroscopy demonstrates minimal elevation of choline (choline:creatinine ratio: 1.3) and lipid/lactate peak. The N-acetylaspartate:creatinine ratio was normal (2.1). (C) White matter tractography from diffusion tensor imaging shows the lesion to lie close to the descending corticospinal tracts. Tracts are seen passing through the area of abnormality around the enhancement; the lesion does not appear to significantly disrupt tracts.

He remained asymptomatic with continuing involution of the lesion at 12 months from the initial presentation. At the last review, 4 years from the initial findings, the child remained stable and asymptomatic, untreated throughout, with further resolution of the lesion and no new lesions in the brain or spine.
evidence_items.temporal_cue: 12 months and 4 years after initial presentation

H&E staining, supplemented by Luxol fast blue staining, confirmed the presence of an inflammatory demyelinating lesion with an obvious transition between preserved white matter and demyelinated white matter. The lesion demonstrated the characteristic radiological features of Baló’s concentric sclerosis, a single tumefactive lesion with a ring-like focus, with concentric areas of T2 hyperintensity and hypointensity.

Immunohistochemistry showed features typical of a demyelinating disorder, including the predominant role for T lymphocytes, with a perivascular distribution but a notable B lymphocyte component.
